# How to Use Duck.ai Chats With Your Own Files for Research Tasks

> **In short:** You can ask Duck.ai questions about a document you already have, such as a report, article, or policy, and then check each answer against the original text. The key rule: the AI can misread or invent details, so always verify before you rely on an answer.

By the end of this guide, you'll be able to bring a document into a Duck.ai conversation, ask specific questions about it, and confirm every answer against the source. This is for anyone who reads long material for work, school, or personal decisions and wants a faster way to find what matters.

## Before you start

- **You already use Duck.ai.** This guide assumes you can open a chat and send a message.
- **A document you're allowed to use.** A text file, a Word file, or a PDF you can open on your device. Avoid anything with sensitive personal, medical, or financial details unless you've read Duck.ai's privacy information and are comfortable with it.
- **Time:** about 20 minutes for your first run through.
- **Limits:** Duck.ai may cap how much you can send or how many chats you can use. Check the Duck.ai site if something seems blocked.

## Step 1 — Check how your document can reach the chat

Before you copy anything, look at the message box at the bottom of the chat. Some versions may have an **attachment button** next to it, often a paperclip-style icon, which lets you choose a file from your device. If you see one, you can attach your document directly.

If you don't see any attachment option, you can still work with the document by pasting the text in. Open your file, select the passage you care about, and copy it. Start with one to three pages at a time, because very long text can get cut short or lose detail.

Whichever route you take, the first thing to do is confirm the document is really in your hands. Open it, scroll to the section you want, and make sure the words on screen match what you expect.

💬 Example: a sentence you might paste in front of your text: "Here is part of a report from my team about [topic]. Read it and wait for my questions."

You'll know it worked when your chat shows either a file name attached to your message or the pasted text sitting in the message box, ready to send.

## Step 2 — Send the document with a clear label

Now send your document. If you attached a file, type a short note in the message box so the AI knows what you're giving it. If you pasted text, put your label above the pasted passage.

A label matters because it tells the AI what to focus on and what to ignore. Say what the document is, who wrote it if that's known, and what date or version it is. Keep it factual. You're not asking the AI to judge the document, just to hold it in context for later questions.

It's also worth saying the AI should use only what you provided. Some chatbots mix in general knowledge, which can blur the line between your source and the AI's own guesses.

💬 Example: "Here is the text of [document name], version [number] from [year]. Use only this text to answer my questions, and tell me if something isn't covered."

If the reply starts summarizing the document, that's a good sign it has read it. If the reply says it can't see anything, the file didn't go through. Try pasting the text instead.

You'll know it worked when the reply mentions the title or main topic of your document, showing the AI has your material in front of it.

## Step 3 — Ask one specific question with a source request

Vague questions get vague answers. Instead of "What's this about?", ask about one specific point and tell the AI to show where the answer comes from.

Type your question in the message box and send it. The reply will usually appear below your message after a short pause, sometimes as a list or a few paragraphs. Read it slowly and note any claim that would matter if it turned out to be wrong.

Asking for the exact sentence from the source is the most useful habit you can build. It turns a claim you have to trust into one you can check in about 30 seconds. If the AI can't point to a sentence, treat that as a warning sign.

💬 Example: "Using only the text I shared, what does the document say about [topic]? Quote the exact sentence you based your answer on."

If the answer is long or wanders off-topic, ask it to shorten the answer or limit it to the one section you pasted. If it doesn't quote anything, ask again and say, "Please give me the exact sentence."

You'll know it worked when your reply includes a quoted sentence you can find in your original document.

## Step 4 — Build on earlier answers in the same chat

Once you have a grounded answer, use the same chat for follow-up questions. The AI can refer back to what it already said, so you don't have to re-paste the document each time. This is a multi-step technique: each question builds on the last one.

For example, start broad, then narrow down. First ask for the main points, then ask for numbers, dates, or names only. Finally, ask how two points relate. Keep each step small so that every answer is easy to check.

Keep in mind that a long chat can drift. If the replies start to feel off-topic, or if the AI seems to forget something you pasted, start a new chat and paste the most important passage again.

💬 Example: "From your last answer, list every number you mentioned and the sentence in my text that each number came from."

If the answer no longer matches your document, don't correct it by arguing. Say, "That doesn't appear in my text. Please remove it and only use the passage I gave you."

You'll know it worked when each follow-up answer points back to a specific part of the document you shared.

## Step 5 — Verify every answer against the original

This is the most important step. AI tools can misread a sentence, blend two ideas, or produce a plausible detail that isn't in your file at all. Duck.ai, like any AI chat, can make these mistakes, so verification is part of the workflow, not an optional extra.

Take the quoted sentence the AI gave you and search for it in your original document. On a computer, use the find shortcut (Ctrl+F on Windows, Command+F on a Mac) and paste the sentence. On a phone, many reading apps have a search icon that works the same way. If the exact words aren't found, the AI may have paraphrased, so read the surrounding paragraph to confirm the meaning.

Check the claim, not just the quote. Does the sentence really say what the AI said it does? Mark any answer you can't confirm as unverified.

💬 Example: "Which of your claims did you not find word-for-word in my text? Mark each one as 'not in source'."

If you can't find the quote, don't trust the answer. Ask the AI to show its reasoning, and go back to the document yourself. Your own reading is the final authority.

You'll know it worked when every answer you keep has a matching sentence you have personally found in the original.

## Step 6 — Save what you verified

A good research habit is to keep a short record of what you confirmed. Chats can get long and hard to scroll, so move only the verified points into a separate place. A notes app, a document, or even a plain text file on your device works well.

For each point, write three things: the claim in your own words, the sentence from the original, and where it appears (page or section). This simple format lets you reuse your research later without re-reading the whole chat. It also makes it easy to share findings with a colleague or classmate.

Duck.ai may or may not offer ways to rename or organize chats, and that can change over time, so don't depend on the chat history as your only record. Your notes are the safer archive.

💬 Example: "Summary: [claim in your words]. Source sentence: [paste exact sentence]. Location: [page or section]."

You'll know it worked when you have a short list of confirmed points you could show someone else, each with a sentence and location next to it.

## Common mistakes

- **Trusting an answer without a quote.** The mistake is accepting a confident-sounding reply. The fix is to always ask for the exact sentence, then search for it in the original.
- **Pasting a huge document all at once.** Long text can be cut short or lose detail, so the AI may answer from only part of it. The fix is to work in sections of one to three pages and say which section you're asking about.
- **Letting one long chat drift.** After many messages, replies can become unfocused or forget earlier material. The fix is to start a new chat, paste the key passage again, and ask your next question there.

## What this means for you

- **In everyday life:** Paste the terms of a lease, a school handbook, or a long article, and ask for the three most important points. Then check each one against the original before you act on it.
- **For your business or work:** Load a meeting transcript or a project report and ask for decisions, deadlines, and owners, each tied to a quoted sentence. Verified notes make handoffs far clearer.
- **If you want to go further:** Try comparing two documents in one chat by pasting each one with a clear label, then asking where they agree and where they conflict, always with quoted sentences. Be extra careful here, because the AI may blur the two sources, so verify every point against both originals.

## Try it now

Open a Duck.ai chat, paste one short paragraph from a document you already have, and send this: "Using only the text I shared, what is the main point? Quote the exact sentence you based it on." Then search for that quote in your original. If it's there, you've just completed the full workflow.
